issues.legal_issue: A bona fide arrangement among family members to settle existing or apprehended disputes may operate as a family arrangement and recognize an interest in property even where the recipient had no enforceable antecedent title to that property.
material_facts: A family document settled competing claims among members of different branches concerning their status and rights in family properties, including properties held in individual names.

The document recognized that one family member was entitled to a half share in a house, although he had been adopted into another branch and lacked an enforceable legal claim to property acquired by his birth father.
Read as a whole, the document’s recitals and operative terms showed conflicts of interest and a bona fide settlement of existing or apprehended disputes among family members.
issues.conclusion: The document was a valid family arrangement, and the family member acquired the recognized half share in the house under it.
issues.legal_principle: Under Pullaiah v. Narasimham, A.I.R. 1966 S.C. 1837, bona fide present or possible disputes, even if they do not involve enforceable legal claims, can support a family arrangement; such an arrangement may also be made to maintain peace or harmony, if its terms are fair in the circumstances. Sahu Madho Das v. Mukund Ram, [1955] 2 S.C.R. 22, and Rani Mewa Kuwar v. Rani Hulas Kuwar, (1873–74) L.R. 1 I.A. 157 at 166, explain that an arrangement proceeds on an assumption of antecedent title, which need not actually exist in law. The arrangement must be assessed as a whole; disputes need not concern every item or pit every participant against every other participant. Williams v. Williams, (1867) 2 Ch. A. 294, was referred to on family arrangements and the relevance of motive and consideration.

predicates.family_members_settling_property_claims: Members of a family made an arrangement addressing competing claims to family property.
predicates.bona_fide_family_claims_or_counterclaims: Family members made bona fide claims or counterclaims that threatened or could threaten family harmony or property interests.
predicates.whole_arrangement_settles_existing_or_ap: Considered as a whole, the arrangement resolved disputes that existed or were apprehended among family members.
predicates.arrangement_valid_as_family_settlement_a: The arrangement is valid as a family settlement and gives its recipient the interest allocated to that recipient.

issues.definition: When family members make a bona fide arrangement that, viewed as a whole, settles existing or apprehended property disputes, the arrangement is valid as a family settlement and confers the allocated interest.

issues.legal_issue: A co-sharer’s title is not extinguished by adverse possession where the alleged adverse possession is effectively interrupted by the co-sharer’s acts of possession during the claimed period.
material_facts: The dispute concerned alleged adverse possession by one co-sharer against another, whose possession in law was also the possession of the other co-sharer unless ouster was established.

The alleged adverse possessor openly asserted a claim to the whole house and enjoyed it, but the other co-sharer stayed in the house on different occasions and openly asserted his title in a municipal survey entry made after that claim.
The other co-sharer’s evidence of staying in the house was corroborated, and his assertion of title and acts of possession were accepted by the trial court and the High Court Single Judge.
The Supreme Court held that these acts interrupted the continuity and exclusiveness of the alleged adverse possession; the other co-sharer’s stays were not merely visits as a guest.
issues.conclusion: The alleged adverse possession did not extinguish the co-sharer’s title, and the Supreme Court restored the decree recognizing that title.
issues.legal_principle: Adverse possession must be adequate, continuous, and exclusive, and the burden of proving those characteristics rests on the adverse possessor: Kuthali Moothavar v. Paringati Kunharankutty, (1921) 48 I.A. 395 at 404. Between co-sharers, adverse possession requires ouster through an open assertion of hostile title coupled with exclusive possession and enjoyment to the other co-sharer’s knowledge: Lakshmi Reddy v. Lakshmi Reddy, [1957] S.C.R. 195 at 202, and Mohammad Baqar v. Naim-un-Nisa Bibi, A.I.R. 1956 S.C. 548. Once possession has become adverse by ouster, a mere assertion of joint title does not interrupt it; effective re-entry or resumption of possession is required: Wuntakal Yalpi Chenabasavana Gowd v. Y. Mahabaleshwarappa, [1955] 1 S.C.R. 131 at 138. A mere stay as a guest is insufficient: Ammakannu Ammal v. Naravanaswami Mudaliar, A.I.R. 1923 Mad. 633. Acts of possession by the title holder may nevertheless interrupt the continuity or exclusiveness required for adverse possession.

predicates.co_sharer_adverse_possession_dispute: The dispute concerns one co-sharer’s claim to have acquired another co-sharer’s title through adverse possession.
predicates.other_co_sharer_claimed_exclusive_hostil: One co-sharer claimed exclusive possession of the property and asserted a hostile claim against the other co-sharer.
predicates.title_holder_effectively_reentered_or_re: The co-sharer whose title was challenged effectively re-entered the property or resumed possession during the claimed period.
predicates.title_holder_stayed_and_openly_asserted_: The co-sharer whose title was challenged stayed in the property and openly asserted ownership during the claimed period.
predicates.co_sharer_title_not_extinguished_by_adve: The co-sharer’s title remains unextinguished by the other co-sharer’s adverse possession.

issues.definition: In a co-sharer adverse-possession dispute, the title remains unextinguished when the alleged exclusive hostile possession is interrupted by the title holder’s effective return to possession or by staying in the property while openly asserting title.
